title: Training 1: Goals and how to combine them

blocks.markdown:
## Different goals, different training

Fitness isn't one thing. This course separates four qualities you can train with weights and a mat, plus the aerobic engine covered in Module 7.

- **Strength:** how much force you can produce, for example the heaviest weight you can lift once.
- **Hypertrophy:** muscle growth, meaning bigger muscle fibres.
- **Muscular endurance:** how long or how many times a muscle can keep working.

blocks.alt: Four quadrants around 'you': strength (heavy, few reps), hypertrophy (close to failure), muscular endurance (light, many reps), mobility (range, control), ringed by aerobic fitness (Module 7).
blocks.caption: Four trainable qualities, plus the engine

blocks.markdown:
## The fourth: mobility

**Mobility** is the ability to move a joint actively through its full range, with control. It's not the same as flexibility, which is how far a joint can be moved passively. Module 8 covers both, along with core and yoga.

## They overlap

The qualities aren't separate boxes. Lifting for muscle also makes you stronger. Strength helps endurance. A goblet squat trains all four a little. What changes with your goal is the emphasis: the load, the reps, and how much time each quality gets in the week.

**What this means for your training:** with fat loss, muscle and strength as your goals, your sessions will mainly train hypertrophy and strength, with mobility and core in the warm-up, and your sport covering endurance.

cards.back: Growth of muscle fibres, leading to bigger muscles.
Mobility: active, controlled range of motion. Flexibility: passive range, how far a joint can be moved.

questions.stem: Which quality does 'the heaviest weight you can lift once' describe?
questions.explanation: That's maximal strength, often measured as a one-repetition maximum (1RM).

lessons.title: Strength vs muscle: the rep ranges

blocks.markdown:
## The old rule, updated

You may have heard 'low reps for strength, 8–12 for size, 15+ for endurance'. The evidence now says something more useful: muscle grows across a wide range of loads, as long as each set ends close to failure. Strength, however, is still built best with heavier loads.

Loads are often given as a percentage of your **1RM**, your one-repetition maximum: the most you can lift once with good form.

blocks.alt: Bar from heavy to light with reps of 1–5, 6–12 and 12–30. Maximal strength peaks at the heavy end, muscle growth spans about 6–30 reps near failure, muscular endurance sits at the light end.
blocks.caption: Loads, reps and what they build

blocks.markdown:
## What the 2026 ACSM position stand recommends

- **Strength:** heavier loads, around 80% of 1RM or more, for 2–3 sets per exercise.
- **Muscle growth:** about 10 sets per muscle group per week, with a wide range of loads.
- **Power:** 30–70% of 1RM, lifted as fast as possible.
- Training to complete failure, and free weights versus machines, made no consistent difference for most healthy adults.

## What it means with a 10 kg dumbbell

In a 2017 meta-analysis, light loads (60% of 1RM or less) built about as much muscle as heavy ones when sets went close to failure, but gave smaller strength gains. Very light loads, around 20% of 1RM, built less muscle. So with light dumbbells you can still grow muscle by taking sets to roughly 15–30 hard reps. For real strength in big lower-body lifts, you'll need heavier weights. That's a key question for Module 3.
**What this means for your training:** light weights aren't wasted: push each set close to failure and they'll build muscle. To build strength, plan heavier kit for the legs and hips.

cards.back: One-repetition maximum: the heaviest load you can lift once with good form. Loads are often given as a % of 1RM.
Muscle grows across ~6–30 reps if sets end close to failure; strength grows best with heavier loads (≥ ~80% 1RM, few reps).

questions.stem: You can do 25 hard goblet squats with your heaviest dumbbell. Which goal does that set suit best?
options: Nothing; it's too light to help
questions.explanation: Sets close to failure at 15–30 reps can build muscle and endurance, but they're too light to drive maximal strength.

questions.stem: What does the 2026 ACSM position stand suggest for muscle growth?
options: About 10 sets per muscle group per week, across a wide range of loads
questions.explanation: Weekly sets matter more than a fixed rep range; failure and machine vs free weights made no consistent difference.

lessons.title: Fat loss: energy balance, and why lifting matters

blocks.markdown:
## Energy in, energy out

Body fat goes down when, over weeks, you use more energy than you eat. That gap is a **calorie deficit**. Exercise helps by raising energy out, but food decides most of the balance. It's much easier to eat 300 kcal than to burn them.

blocks.alt: Scale: food against resting metabolism (largest), daily movement, exercise and digestion. In the same deficit, diet only loses fat and some muscle; diet plus lifting loses fat and keeps muscle.
blocks.caption: Energy balance, and what lifting protects

blocks.markdown:
## In a deficit, lifting protects muscle

When you eat less, the body can lose muscle as well as fat. Lifting tells it the muscle is still needed. In a 2022 meta-analysis, people training in a deficit kept their strength gains, but gained less **lean mass** (everything except fat) than people eating enough. Deficits of about 500 kcal a day or more stopped lean-mass gains altogether.

## A sensible pace

A common guide for keeping muscle is to lose about 0.5–1% of body weight a week. For an 80 kg person, that's 0.4–0.8 kg a week. Faster means more muscle at risk and harder training. Module 9 covers the details: protein, food choices and tracking.
**What this means for your training:** for fat loss, combine a moderate deficit with 2–3 strength sessions a week. The lifting decides whether the weight you lose is mostly fat.

cards.back: Using more energy than you eat over time, which reduces body fat.
Everything in the body except fat: muscle, bone, organs, water.

questions.stem: Two people lose 5 kg on the same diet. One also lifts weights 3 times a week. What's the likely difference?
options: None; weight lost is weight lost
The lifter loses a larger share as fat and keeps more muscle
The lifter can eat without limits
questions.explanation: Resistance training signals the body to keep muscle in a deficit, so more of the loss is fat.

blocks.markdown:
## Sources

1. **Meta-analysis** — Murphy C, Koehler K, Energy deficiency impairs resistance training gains in lean mass but not strength, Scand J Med Sci Sports 2022;32(1):125–137.
2. **Review** — Helms ER, Aragon AA, Fitschen PJ, Evidence-based recommendations for natural bodybuilding contest preparation, J Int Soc Sports Nutr 2014;11:20 (0.5–1% of body weight a week).
3. **Image** — own diagram.

## Not a contest

**Aerobic training**, or cardio, means sustained activity that raises your heart rate and breathing: running, cycling, swimming, most sports. Resistance training works muscles against a load. They do different jobs, and the WHO recommends both for adults.

blocks.alt: Table comparing cardio, weights and both. Cardio is strongest for energy used and heart and lungs, weights for muscle, strength and bone, and both are best overall.
blocks.caption: What each type of training does best

blocks.markdown:
## What a long trial showed

In an 8-month trial in adults with overweight (STRRIDE AT/RT), cardio reduced body weight and fat more than resistance training. Resistance training added lean mass, which cardio didn't. The combination reduced fat about as much as cardio and added lean mass, but took about twice the training time.

## The WHO minimums

- 150–300 minutes a week of moderate aerobic activity, or 75–150 minutes of vigorous activity, or a mix of both.
- Muscle-strengthening activities for all major muscle groups on 2 or more days a week.
- Less time sitting.

Your sport 1–2 times a week covers much of the aerobic part already.
**What this means for your training:** keep your sport as your cardio base, and add 2–3 short strength sessions. That covers both WHO recommendations and all three of your goals.

cards.back: Sustained activity that raises heart rate and breathing (running, cycling, sports). Builds the heart, lungs and endurance.
150–300 min moderate (or 75–150 min vigorous) aerobic activity a week, plus muscle strengthening on ≥2 days.

questions.stem: Which statement matches the STRRIDE AT/RT trial?
options: Weights alone lost the most fat
Cardio lost more fat; weights added lean mass; combining them did both
There was no difference between groups
questions.explanation: Cardio was better for fat and body mass, weights for lean mass; the combination gave both, at about double the time.

## The interference effect

For years, coaches warned that cardio 'kills your gains'. The idea is the **interference effect**: endurance training blunting the results of strength training. **Concurrent training** means doing both in the same programme, and it's what you'll be doing.

blocks.alt: Effect of adding cardio to strength training: almost zero on muscle size and maximal strength; a small negative effect on explosive strength, mainly with sessions within 20 minutes of each other.
blocks.caption: Does cardio hurt strength gains? Meta-analysis results

blocks.markdown:
## What the evidence says

A 2021 meta-analysis of 43 studies found that combining cardio with strength training didn't reduce muscle growth or maximal strength gains. It did slightly reduce gains in **explosive strength**, the ability to produce force fast, as in jumps and sprints. That effect appeared when the two were done within 20 minutes of each other, and not when they were at least 3 hours apart. The order within a session made no clear difference.

## Fitting it around your sport

Football and tennis need explosive strength, so spacing matters a little more for you.

- Put strength sessions on non-sport days, or at least 3 hours away from sport.
- Avoid a hard leg session the day before a match.
- If you must combine them, keep them in the order you prefer: the evidence doesn't favour one.
**What this means for your training:** cardio won't stop you building muscle or strength. Space your strength sessions away from football and tennis, and keep hard leg work away from match days.

cards.back: Endurance training blunting strength-training results. In recent meta-analyses: no effect on muscle size or max strength, a small effect on explosive strength when sessions are close together.
Doing endurance and strength training in the same programme.

questions.stem: You play tennis on Tuesday evening. When is the best slot for a strength session?
options: Monday or Wednesday, or Tuesday morning at least 3 hours before
questions.explanation: Explosive-strength interference appeared with sessions within 20 minutes, not with 3 or more hours apart.

blocks.markdown:
## Sources

1. **Meta-analysis** — Schumann M et al., Compatibility of concurrent aerobic and strength training for skeletal muscle size and function: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis, Sports Med 2021 (doi:10.1007/s40279-021-01587-7).
2. **Image** — own diagram.

lessons.title: Losing fat and gaining muscle at once

blocks.markdown:
## Body recomposition

Usually, losing fat means a deficit, and gaining muscle needs enough food, so the two pull in opposite directions. **Body recomposition** is doing both at once: the scale may barely move while your waist shrinks and your muscles grow.

blocks.alt: Same body weight over 12 weeks: less fat, more muscle afterwards. Most likely in people new to lifting, returning after a break or with higher body fat, with enough protein and progressive training.
blocks.caption: Body recomposition: same weight, different body

blocks.markdown:
## Who it works for

A 2020 review found recomposition well documented in three groups: people new to lifting, people returning after a break, and people with more body fat. It's also possible in trained people. In every group it needs two things: enough protein, and progressive resistance training. Someone with a sports background who has never lifted properly is a good candidate.

## Why the scale misleads

If you lose fat and gain muscle, your weight can stay flat for weeks. Track your waist, photos and strength alongside body weight (Lesson 0.5). And keep the deficit moderate: large deficits stall muscle gain (Lesson 3).

**What this means for your training:** you can aim for fat loss and muscle gain at the same time. Keep the deficit moderate, eat enough protein, add load week by week, and judge progress by your waist and strength, not just the scale.

cards.back: Losing fat and gaining muscle at the same time. Most likely in beginners, returners and people with more body fat; needs protein and progressive training.
If you lose fat and gain muscle, weight can stay flat for weeks. Track waist, photos and strength alongside it.

questions.stem: After 8 weeks, your weight is unchanged, your waist is 3 cm smaller and your push-ups went from 15 to 22. What's most likely?
options: Nothing is changing; increase the deficit sharply
questions.explanation: A smaller waist plus rising strength at stable weight is the classic recomposition pattern.

blocks.markdown:
## Sources

1. **Review** — Barakat C et al., Body recomposition: can trained individuals build muscle and lose fat at the same time?, Strength Cond J 2020;42(5):7–21.
2. **Meta-analysis** — Murphy C, Koehler K, Scand J Med Sci Sports 2022;32(1):125–137.
3. **Image** — own diagram.

## One priority at a time

You can train for several things, but one should lead each 12-week block. The priority decides what gets the best slot in the session and what gives way when time is short. With three short sessions a week, you can't chase everything at full speed.

blocks.alt: Goal card with five lines: 12-week priority, outcome measure (waist), performance measures (goblet squat, push-ups), behaviour targets (sessions, protein, steps), reviews at weeks 4, 8 and 12.
blocks.caption: Your 12-week goal card

blocks.markdown:
## Make it measurable

A useful goal is specific, measurable and has a date. Mix three kinds of target:

1. **Outcome:** what you want to change, for example your waist.
2. **Performance:** what you'll be able to do, for example reps or load.
3. **Behaviour:** what you'll do every week, for example sessions, steps and protein.

Behaviour targets are the ones you control directly, so they deserve the most attention.

## An example (illustrative)

- **Priority:** fat loss while keeping and building muscle.
- **Outcome:** waist down 3–4 cm in 12 weeks.
- **Performance:** goblet squat from 20 to 30 reps at 12 kg, then move to a heavier kettlebell; push-ups from 15 to 25.
- **Behaviour:** 3 strength sessions of 30 minutes a week, sport once or twice, 8,000+ steps a day.

Your own numbers come from your baseline tests.
**What this means for your training:** fill in a goal card now, using your baseline. Review it at weeks 4, 8 and 12, and let Modules 5–6 turn it into a programme.

cards.back: Outcome (what changes), performance (what you can do), behaviour (what you do each week). Behaviour is the part you control.
One goal leads each 12-week block: it gets the best slot in the session, and the rest give way when time is short.

questions.explanation: Behaviour targets describe actions you control each week; the others are outcomes or performance.
